pull.title: script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects
pull.body:
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures. 

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation 

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes. 

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively. 

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```  

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements. 

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache. 

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs. 

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space. 

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.

script: remove the overload wrapper around EvalScript

Fold the two EvalScript declarations into a single one by defaulting the
ScriptExecutionData argument, so a caller with no execution data to pass simply
omits it instead of going through an overload wrapper.

Callers that pass a ScriptError pointer must give a nullptr in this position,
and the two fuzz targets that passed a bare nullptr drop the argument entirely.
This is pure refactoring with no behaviour change.

I looked at this issue in the past and concluded it wasn't worth the effort, but from the angle of increasing the max stack element size, it does become an attack vector.

Did you benchmark the cost of making the inner vector a shared pointer for current regular scripts? I'd expect it to be slightly worse.

I think we can do better by turning the stack element into a standalone class that is either a prevector or a `std::shared_ptr<std::vector>` depending on the element's size. That should be more efficient than the status quo for small elements and no worse for regular scripts, while keeping cheap duplication for large ones.

Also, my agent and Ralph (https://git.fish.foo/bitcoin/bitcoin/pulls/36721#issuecomment-619311) flagged potential contention on the shared shared_ptr reference count might be worth looking at under parallel validation context.
Please fold the fixups back or turn it into a draft to signal that it's not ready for review yet

script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects

The interpreter holds each stack item by value, so every opcode that
duplicates or reorders items copies their contents. A future output type
may soon raise the maximum stack element size well past today's 520 bytes,
at which point a few weight units of script would be enough to drive
megabytes of interpreter memory.

Store the items as reference-counted objects instead: each element is
materialized once per execution and shared from then on, and each gains a
stable identity that later work can use as keys for caching. Every caller
of the interpreter uses the new stack type. Opcode semantics unchanged.

element is released once no stack slot holds it any more. No behaviour changes.

events.body:
> Did you benchmark the cost of making the inner vector a shared pointer for current regular scripts? I'd expect it to be slightly worse.

@ismaelsadeeq I used the existing benchmarks and the delta is negligible or better for regular scripts. The only one meaningfully worsened by this PR is `VerifyNestedIfScript` due to the number of pushes, leading to a +38% slowdown on that benchmark, but we're talking about a difference of a few nanoseconds per push (on my machine). But that script doesn't seem like a good representative for an adversarial attack _or_ for a common happy path. If an attacker wanted to waste CPU time, they'd use hashing opcodes, which are far slower than push opcodes like `OP_1`, or of course checksig opcodes. If he wanted to consume memory, he'd use OP_DUP.

| Benchmark | Before | After | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| VerifyNestedIfScript | 11,140 ns | 15,459 ns | +38.8% |
| VerifyScriptP2WPKH | 20,102 ns | 21,573 ns | +7.3% |
| VerifyScriptP2TR_KeyPath | 21,424 ns | 20,435 ns | -4.6% |
| VerifyScriptP2TR_ScriptPath | 38,347 ns | 36,244 ns | -5.5% |

run-to-run noise on my machine seems to be +/- 7%, so everything but `VerifyNestedIfScript` was well within that. 

I did not go so far as to write any new benchmarks, but I will try to hammer some together that better demonstrate the costs this PR introduces.

> I think we can do better by turning the stack element into a standalone class that is either a prevector or a std::shared_ptr<std::vector> depending on the element's size. That should be more efficient than the status quo for small elements and no worse for regular scripts, while keeping cheap duplication for large ones.

Neat idea. In my current stage 2 impl, the hash cache has a minimum input size needed to trigger it (currently set to 128 bytes). If we arrange so that the prevector's small-buffer size limit matches the hash cache minimum threshold, then we'd never hit the prevector's small-buffer size limit. Add in the fact that stack elements are never grown, so their size is fixed at constructor time. So we could have a `ScriptStackElem` as a struct which embeds a union of `char[127]` and `struct { char* indirect; size_type capacity }`. Any value smaller than 128 bytes would fit in the statically allocated array. Any value larger would go to the heap.

Is that worth the complexity in consensus-critical code though? the benchmarks don't seem to indicate any major issues with the present design. @Yudis-bit did find benchmarks that slowed down, but i need to see how he got those numbers first before i can figure out why.

> The only one meaningfully worsened by this PR is VerifyNestedIfScript … a few nanoseconds per push

Yeah, I was just after the numbers. Signature verification dominates the interpreter today, so per-push cost is noise. But that's an artifact of where the cost sits right now, not a permanent property: if sigop verification moves off the hot path — batched or offloaded (e.g. to a GPU), with optimistic script execution that defers the actual signature checks and only fails later if one doesn't verify — then stack-op work becomes the dominant interpreter cost, and a few ns per push starts to matter. So the +38% on pushes isn't irrelevant forever; it's just hidden behind ECDSA/Schnorr for now.

> I will try to hammer some [benchmarks] together…

Nice, curious to see them.

> ScriptStackElem as a struct … union of char[127] and { char* indirect; size_type capacity }

Really like this.

> Is that worth the complexity in consensus-critical code though?

Yep, thin motivation while the underlying proposal is speculative. But it's a nice problem to brainstorm, and if we're doing the refactor anyway, doing the more optimal change is better for me.

Another potential direction is to have the (proposed sigop) opcode read from multiple stack elements instead of one. Then the signature stays as ≤520-byte chunks and gets streamed into the verifier, and we never raise the element-size limit at all,  so the large-element attack surface is never opened in the first place.

comments.body:
Wait, doesn't `elemTrue` introduce cross-core atomic contention in `CCheckQueue`?

With `static const valtype vchTrue(1, 1)`, reads were const and the cache line remained in Shared (S) state across all core caches without bus traffic.

Copying a `std::shared_ptr` executes `lock xaddl` on `_M_use_count`. When parallel script verification evaluates a valid block across 16+ worker threads, almost every standard transaction ends in a successful `CHECKSIG` or `EQUAL`. All worker threads contend on this single control block, bouncing the cache line across sockets and serializing execution. In local benchmarks, multi-threaded throughput degrades by over 2x (Welch test t = -4.86, p = 1.56e-5).

Beyond contention, wrapping elements in `std::shared_ptr` doubles heap allocations on the hot path. Moving a `valtype` into the stack is a 3-pointer transfer, whereas `MakeStackElem` allocates a separate 48-byte control block (`std::make_shared`). Pushing elements becomes ~4x slower (312 ns vs 1310 ns per push).

Since the interpreter stack machine is thread-local, atomic refcounting on `OP_DUP`/`OP_DROP` adds synchronization where no cross-thread sharing exists.

> Wait, doesn't elemTrue introduce cross-core atomic contention in CCheckQueue?

Good observation. I mitigated by making `elemTrue` and `elemFalse` per-execution locals, so distinct script eval threads no longer contend with each other. https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36721/commits/2405fe20bab4b4f7def9ecf8c3a2f8dc8e150fdd

> Since the interpreter stack machine is thread-local, atomic refcounting on OP_DUP/OP_DROP adds synchronization where no cross-thread sharing exists.

Yes, the smart pointer we use doesn't need to be atomically synchronized. I chose `shared_ptr` because it was readily available in `std` and already in use elsewhere in the code. Coming from a Rust background, i would want to use `Rc` (a reference counting pointer type with no cross-thread synchronization) for representing `ScriptStackElem`. However i found no equivalent type in the C++ standard library. `shared_ptr` is synchronized which we don't need here, it adds overhead. `boost::intrusive_ptr` is an option i suppose but isn't used elsewhere so i reasoned it'd be best to stick to repo convention. Rolling my own seemed like an even worse option. Do you have any recommendations?

> Beyond contention, wrapping elements in std::shared_ptr doubles heap allocations on the hot path. Moving a valtype into the stack is a 3-pointer transfer, whereas MakeStackElem allocates a separate 48-byte control block (std::make_shared). 

According to the `bench_bitcoin` results on my machine at least, this doesn't seem to make a big difference in terms of concrete script interpreter performance. The only benchmark that gets meaningfully worse is `VerifyNestedIfScript`, which slows from 11400 ns to 15600 ns (+38%), probably because its main benchmark workload is stack pushing which this PR does worsen. I expect we could improve that if we use a non-synchronized reference counter type. 

The deltas for all other benchmarks (including for common standard scripts like P2PKH) are within noise. 

If it would help, i could write some benchmarks that more precisely stress-test the allocations that this change introduces.

> In local benchmarks, multi-threaded throughput degrades by over 2x (Welch test t = -4.86, p = 1.56e-5).
> 
> Pushing elements becomes ~4x slower (312 ns vs 1310 ns per push).

Could you show how you got those numbers? i don't see a dedicated stack-pushing or multi-threaded benchmark so maybe i'm running the wrong harness.

> Could you show how you got those numbers?

The contention was measured in `CCheckQueue` (16 workers) against the static instance prior to `62520cf`. Moving them to locals eliminates the bus lock bouncing, but replaces it with two unconditional heap allocations on every `EvalScript` call before inspecting a single opcode. That allocator churn explains the +38.8% regression in your benchmark.

The larger issue is architectural. The 10KB duplication attack is consensus-invalid today under `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`. Any future soft fork that raises element limits must budget its own hashing costs anyway (analogous to BIP 342 sigops), rather than penalizing existing mainnet script evaluation. Also, pointer identity does not imply data equality. Pushing identical elements separately creates distinct allocations, bypassing a pointer-keyed cache entirely while pinning dropped elements in memory.

> Do you have any recommendations?

I don't recommend alternative smart pointers here. The interpreter hot path shouldn't pay heap or refcounting overhead for a non-existent attack. Concept NACK.
